newsitem.title: TURKMENISTAN: Afghan war blocks central Asia's route to market.
newsitem.headline: Afghan war blocks central Asia's route to market.

text.p: The Afghan war is blocking resource-rich but landlocked Central Asia's route to international markets, Uzbek President Islam Karimov said at a regional economic summit which ended on Wednesday.
"If the war continues in Afghanistan, not one project here means anything," Karimov said at a two-day transport summit of the Economic Cooperation Organisation (ECO) in Turkmenistan.

"The war in Afghanistan has gone on for 18 years," Karimov told leaders from Pakistan, Iran, Turkey, Afghanistan and the ex-Soviet states of Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Turkmenistan.

He accused Pakistan of prolonging the war by aiding the purist Islamic Taleban militia, which now controls three quarters of the country. "It's a tragedy not only for the people of Afghanistan but for the countries neighbouring Afghanistan," he said.

The leaders from 10 Asian states had been trying to find a way of getting vast oil and gas reserves from Central Asia to market and breaking the region's dependence on Russia, which controls the Soviet-era pipeline network.
Iranian, Turkish and Turkmen leaders took a step forward on Wednesday, signing a memorandum to export up to 30 billion cubic metres of natural gas a year from Turkmenistan to Turkey via Iran.
But as with so many other initiatives in the region, there were few details on financing or when gas might begin to flow.

Turkmen President Saparmurat Niyazov said turning Central Asia from its traditional export route north through Russia to the Gulf, Indian Ocean and Mediterranean could cost $40-$50 billion. None of the ECO states have that kind of cash.
A much-trumpeted new rail route south linking the Soviet-built rail network via Turkmenistan through diplomatically isolated Iran is barely functioning.
"The link is carrying no passengers and very little freight," said a Western diplomat based in Ashgabat.
An Iranian-Kazakh oil swaps deal, which could place up to six million tonnes of Kazakh crude on the Gulf, is stalled.
U.S. oil majors cannot invest in oil transport through Iran as the republic is subject to a United States embargo over what Washington says is Tehran's sponsorship of terrorist groups.
Perhaps the most ambitious plan, to build a $2 billion gas pipeline south to Pakistan via Afghanistan, is held up by war.

The pipeline, to be built by U.S. Unocal Corp and Saudi Arabia's Delta Oil, would carry 20 billion cubic metres (bcm) of gas a year, and an oil pipeline would be laid eventually along its 1,500 km (1,000 mile) route.
"It's a waiting game," John Imle, president of Unocal Corp, told Reuters in Ashgabat on Wednesday. "We've been disappointed that Afghanistan remains a country of turmoil."
The Taleban were conspicuous by their absence at the summit, attended by ousted President Burhanuddin Rabbani.

The fall of the Afghan capital Kabul last September to the Taleban sent shock waves through Central Asia, nervous of Islamic fundamentalism and concerned that Afghan tensions could spill over their own borders.
